items.title: William Russell Interview, 1976-02-16
items.q: We were partners in the Hot Record Exchange.

ctx.x: Well, there's a chapter in Jasmine called New Orleans Music. Yeah. Which you did with Stephen Smith. I think you did that. Now, how did you and he decide to do it together? And how did your research? I don't know who suggested that we do it together.

Steve is much interested in New Orleans Music too, of course. We were partners in the Hot Record Exchange. So, actually at that time he got the idea of opening a store then, a retail store, which didn't open until 1939. Right. But he was very busy organizing things. And actually didn't have time really to work on that chapter except his wife did most of the work and she did a lot of the research. Steve and she would go around and interview people. I'd made a couple of trips to Chicago. We even got an advance. I…

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-09-04
items.q: Steve Smith also organized that date.

ctx.x: He received you very ambly, though.

Yeah, very friendly. When Jelly, you see, there was that seniority business, too, that he wouldn't have, Judy, being younger, wouldn't have dared be leader. Once they wanted Jelly to record with Victor, I mean, with Decca, with Louis Armstrong, is what I'm trying to say, when they made that new Arlene's album that Louis made, and Steve Smith also organized that date. The same one that Judy was in, had a band, and the one where they makes the 219 blues. Sidney Bechet was on the date, too. And Jelly was supposed to…
Which place is that now? Music Box. The same place here.

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1975-02-02
items.q: as Steve Smith once said to me, those were the—when we were talking about a certain player.

ctx.x: So anyway, to get back to the point, Gene Williams had heard these records and agreed with me too that at least Bunk showed some possibilities. You couldn't really tell much how he played, both because his lip wasn't in shape and just by himself. The type of trumpet playing that Bunk did, which was a remarkable thing, and yet by itself it wouldn't sound that effective. Bunk was hardly ever on the beat, so if you didn't hear him patting his foot and all there, you could really tell of course where the beat is, but…
Well, of course, we'll never know what Joe Oliver really sounded like.
